tldr: FAM-DQ is a novel aerial manipulator that connects two small quadrotors to the ends of a carbon pipe via passive joints. It uses a long lever arm effect to generate high torque while achieving fully actuated 6-DoF decoupled control of position and attitude.
hero_caption: Overall structure of FAM-DQ. It consists of two quadrotor propulsion modules attached to both ends of a central frame via passive joints, along with a central servo-driven end-effector. Using the long frame as a lever, it generates high interaction torque without adding active tilt mechanisms.
overview:
In aerial physical interaction (APhI) tasks using drones, operations like turning valves or tightening screws demand high interaction torques. However, conventional underactuated systems—mounting a robotic arm on a standard drone—suffer from strong coupling between translational and rotational dynamics, limiting control precision and disturbance rejection during contact. On the other hand, fully actuated platforms with tilted rotors decouple position and attitude control, but they face a dilemma: active tilt mechanisms add significant weight, and short geometric moment arms prevent them from delivering sufficient torque.

To solve this, the authors proposed "FAM-DQ," a design that places two small quadrotors at both ends of a central frame (carbon pipe) via passive joints. Using the frame itself as a physical lever (moment arm), it substantially amplifies the torque generated by module thrust while eliminating the extra servo weight of active tilting. In addition, the central end-effector is equipped with a gear-driven servo, which combines with the frame's roll angle to achieve omnidirectional pointing and fully decoupled 6-DoF control.

In hardware experiments, FAM-DQ achieved decoupled control unique to fully actuated platforms, tracking circular trajectories with fixed attitude and swinging its attitude by 30 degrees without shifting position. The team also conducted static torque measurements and screw-driving tasks with an M8 bolt. The system produced a high torque of up to 1.019 N·m with a total mass of just 0.447 kg, reaching a torque-to-mass ratio of 2.28 N·m/kg. This demonstrates a simple, effective approach for demanding high-torque aerial tasks.
contributions: Proposed a fully actuated aerial manipulator mechanism that links two quadrotors to the ends of a central frame via passive joints, significantly amplifying torque through the lever principle.
Combined an asymmetric joint topology (different DoF on each side) with an end-effector pointing servo to achieve both 6-DoF fully actuated decoupled control and omnidirectional manipulation.
Constructed a lightweight cascaded control architecture and control allocation method that hierarchically separates the propulsion modules' fast internal dynamics from the overall system control.
Demonstrated in real-world experiments complete decoupling of position and attitude, a torque output of 1.019 N·m at a total mass of 0.447 kg, and practical screw driving.

sections.heading: The Aerial Interaction Dilemma: Underactuated Coupling vs. Fully Actuated Torque Limits
sections.summary: Applying aerial manipulation to demanding tasks like bolt fastening requires both high interaction torques and precise 6-DoF end-effector control. However, existing underactuated setups, tilted-rotor platforms, and multi-drone cooperative systems face coupling, added weight, or extreme dynamic complexity. This paper introduces FAM-DQ, which pairs two quadrotors with passive joints to leverage a moment-arm effect.
sections.details:
As drones evolve from passive sensing platforms into active contact agents performing Aerial Physical Interaction (APhI), expectations are rising for high-torque tasks like turning valves or tightening bolts. However, conventional underactuated systems—mounting an arm on a standard multicopter—suffer from strong dynamic coupling between translation and rotation, as generating horizontal thrust requires tilting the body. This fundamentally restricts end-effector positioning accuracy and contact disturbance rejection.

To address this, researchers have explored fully actuated and overactuated platforms with non-coplanar tilted rotors. While these can decouple position and attitude to exert forces in arbitrary directions, active tilting servos or complex multi-rotor airframes add parasitic mass, compromising payload capacity and flight endurance. Furthermore, their geometric moment arms are constrained by vehicle dimensions, causing actuators to saturate rapidly when resisting large reaction torques.

Multi-agent cooperative systems linking multiple flight units have also been proposed. However, their kinematics and dynamics become extraordinarily complex, making reliable attitude control and trajectory tracking difficult to guarantee in real-world environments.

The authors therefore devised "FAM-DQ," mounting two quadrotors at opposite ends of a central frame via passive joints. Using the central rod as a physical lever, the platform efficiently transforms rotor thrust into end-effector torque, realizing both 6-DoF full actuation and high torque output within a simple mechanical architecture.

sections.heading: Efficient Hardware Powered by Lever Principles and Asymmetric Passive Joints
sections.summary: FAM-DQ connects propulsion modules to both ends of a high-rigidity carbon pipe via passive joints and places a gear-driven servo end-effector at the center. By adopting an asymmetric topology with different degrees of freedom on each side, it balances arbitrary end-effector pointing and torque generation without redundant mechanisms.
sections.details:
The core concept of FAM-DQ is using the long central frame as a lever arm to efficiently produce large moments from each propulsion module's thrust. By avoiding active tilt servos and minimizing internal force cancellations between rotors, the entire system remains extremely lightweight.

The hardware consists mainly of the central frame, the end-effector, and two propulsion modules:
- Central frame: Built around a high-rigidity carbon fiber tube, it preserves structural stiffness while providing a long moment arm for torque amplification.
- End-effector: Driven by a gear-coupled servo around the main rod, allowing it to point toward workpieces across a wide angular range.
- Asymmetric connection topology: The C-shaped frames connecting the propulsion modules to the rod feature a clever joint structure. On Propulsion Module 1, the C-frame is rigidly fixed to the central rod, and the module connects via a 1-DoF passive revolute joint (pitch axis). On Propulsion Module 2, the C-frame itself can passively rotate around the rod (roll axis) via bearings, while the module connects via an orthogonal passive joint (pitch axis), providing 2 DoF relative to the central frame.

This asymmetric configuration works because Propulsion Module 2 can freely direct its thrust vector in all directions, whereas Propulsion Module 1 is roll-locked to the central axis. Thus, differential thrust torque from Module 1 directly controls the roll attitude of the entire central frame (and roughly points the tool tip). Coordinating this with the central servo allows the end-effector to point in any working direction, while synthesizing thrust vectors from both modules fully generates 6-DoF wrenches (forces and torques).

Each propulsion module is equipped with 1204 5000kV brushless motors, 3015 propellers, an independent flight controller, ESCs, and a battery. They communicate with the central controller in real time over a low-latency wireless link (~10 ms).

captions.F1: Hardware structure of FAM-DQ. Propulsion modules 1 and 2 are mounted at both ends of a central carbon pipe via passive joints. The asymmetric configuration—1-DoF passive joint for Module 1, 2-DoF for Module 2—works in concert with the end-effector servo to achieve fully actuated control.

sections.heading: Two-Stage Modeling: Decoupling Full-System Dynamics from Propulsion Modules
sections.summary: Because torques generated along the long frame dominate the system, the dynamic model is separated into full-system translational/rotational dynamics and individual module rotational dynamics. The relationship between the 6-DoF wrench at the end-effector frame and each module's tilt and thrust is derived explicitly.
sections.details:
Since module thrust produces large torques across the length of the central frame, the equations of motion are divided into global system dynamics and local module dynamics.

### III-A System Dynamics and Allocation
Coordinate systems are defined for the world frame $\mathcal{F}_w$, body frame $\mathcal{F}_b$, end-effector frame $\mathcal{F}_e$, and propulsion module frames $\mathcal{F}_1, \mathcal{F}_2$. Based on Newton-Euler equations, translational and rotational motions are formulated using total mass $M$ and inertia tensor $\boldsymbol{J}$.
Two reasonable assumptions simplify analysis and control:
1. Minor motions of the end-effector have negligible impact on the overall center of mass and inertia tensor.
2. Since the propulsion modules are situated far from the central center of mass, they are approximated as point masses, omitting small variations in overall inertia caused by self-rotation around passive joints.

Total thrust $\boldsymbol{f}^e$ in the end-effector frame $\mathcal{F}_e$ is the vector sum of thrusts from both propulsion modules. Torque $\boldsymbol{\tau}^e$ consists of moments generated by thrust across arm length $L$ plus torque transmission components from the modules. Because the end-effector's axial rotation can be isolated from frame rotation via the servo, independent wrench control equations at the tool tip are cleanly obtained.

### III-B Propulsion Modules Dynamics
Because module translation matches the overall system, only rotational motion is formulated. Each module controls its attitude via rotor thrusts and counter-torques. Crucially, Module 1's roll is rigidly locked to the central frame. As a result, the driving torque $\tau_y^e$ needed to rotate the central frame acts directly on Module 1 as a load disturbance. The paper derives geometric constraint equations for this angular acceleration, providing the foundation for feedforward compensation in the subsequent controller.

captions.F2: Definition of coordinate frames showing geometric relations between the world frame $\mathcal{F}_w$, end-effector frame $\mathcal{F}_e$, body frame $\mathcal{F}_b$, propulsion module frames $\mathcal{F}_1, \mathcal{F}_2$, and C-frame $\mathcal{F}_c$.

sections.heading: Cascaded Control and Algebraic Thrust Allocation Leveraging Full Actuation
sections.summary: The control architecture is cascaded into a global controller calculating target end-effector wrenches and local controllers for each module. By adding an energy-balancing constraint across overactuated degrees of freedom, the system algebraically solves for unique target attitudes and thrusts in real time.
sections.details:
Taking advantage of the system's full actuation, the control framework adopts a hierarchical structure.

### IV-A Global Controller
Based on commands from a high-level planner and current state feedback, position and attitude are computed completely independently.
- Position Controller: Uses cascaded PID control and gravity compensation to generate the required translational force $\boldsymbol{f}^e$ in the end-effector frame from target position $\boldsymbol{p}_d$ and velocity $\boldsymbol{v}_d$.
- Attitude Extraction and Controller: Decomposes target end-effector attitude into the main rod pointing vector $\boldsymbol{q}_d$ and end-effector servo angle $\theta_d$. Because full-system dynamics operate at much lower frequencies than module response bandwidth, rod tilting torques $\tau_x^e, \tau_z^e$ are determined via cascaded PID neglecting nonlinear terms. Torque around the central frame axis $\tau_y^e$ is assigned to Module 1.
- Control Allocation: Maps the required force $\boldsymbol{f}^e$ and torques $\tau_x^e, \tau_z^e$ into thrusts $f_1, f_2$ and tilt angles ($\theta_1, \phi_1, \theta_2, \phi_2$) for both modules. Thrust along the frame axis ($\boldsymbol{y}_b$ axis) is overactuated since either module can produce it. To equalize energy consumption between modules, the authors introduce a constraint enforcing equal axial thrust sharing. This makes it possible to solve the system of equations algebraically. Although two sets of solutions exist for identical thrust vectors, the controller selects the solution closest to current attitudes to avoid abrupt transitions.

### IV-B Propulsion Module Controller
Inside each module, geometric attitude tracking on SO(3) tracks allocated target attitudes $\boldsymbol{R}_{d_i}$ and angular velocities $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{d_i}$. To prevent unwanted constraint torques around passive joint axes from disturbing the system, a projection matrix $(\boldsymbol{I} - \boldsymbol{z}_{c_i}^i {\boldsymbol{z}_{c_i}^i}^T)$ removes torque components along the C-frame axis. Additionally, the driving torque $\tau_{d_1}$ needed to rotate the central frame is superposed onto Module 1 as feedforward, mapping to individual motor speeds via the inverse rotor effectiveness matrix $\boldsymbol{T}^{-1}$.

captions.F3: Overall block diagram of the proposed control system, illustrating the cascaded structure where the global controller computes end-effector wrenches, feeds into control allocation, and issues commands to local geometric attitude control loops on both propulsion modules.

sections.heading: From Decoupled Tracking to Screw Driving: High Torque-to-Mass Ratio Validated
sections.summary: Inside a motion-capture facility, the team conducted circular trajectory tracking, attitude variation during fixed hovering, static torque measurements, and M8 bolt driving. Experiments verified complete position-attitude decoupling and demonstrated an output torque of 1.019 N·m for a 0.447 kg vehicle (2.28 N·m/kg torque-to-mass ratio), successfully completing screw driving.
sections.details:
All experiments were conducted indoors using a motion capture system.

- Position Tracking: The platform tracked a horizontal circular trajectory with a 0.75 m radius while holding its end-effector attitude steady (0 degrees). Position tracking error stayed within $\pm 0.05$ m, and attitude fluctuations remained within $\pm 1.5^{\circ}$, clearly demonstrating fully actuated horizontal translation without vehicle tilt.
- Attitude Tracking: While hovering at a fixed position, FAM-DQ tracked roll commands of $\pm 20^{\circ}$, yaw commands of $\pm 30^{\circ}$, and combined sinusoidal references. Despite slight phase lag from actuator delay, it tracked stably; during aggressive attitude swings, position errors were held to $\pm 0.08$ m in $x$, $\pm 0.05$ m in $y$, and just $\pm 0.02$ m in $z$.
- Static Torque Output: Connecting the tool tip to a wall-mounted precision torque sensor (0.001 N·m resolution), the system ramped up axial torque. It recorded a peak absolute torque of 1.019 N·m. With a total vehicle mass of just 0.447 kg, this yields a torque-to-mass ratio of 2.28 N·m/kg, quantitatively proving its ability to output remarkable torque despite its compact scale.
- Screw Driving: For a practical physical contact task, a screwdriver bit was attached to drive an M8×24 mm socket head cap screw into a workpiece. FAM-DQ approached, aligned with the socket, applied downward pressing force while exerting axial torque, and successfully drove the screw home. Continuous torque output was maintained throughout the physical interaction.

captions.F6: Static torque output test setup. FAM-DQ docks with a wall-mounted torque sensor, producing a large torque of up to 1.019 N·m relative to its 0.447 kg mass.
captions.F7: Aerial screw-driving experiment showing FAM-DQ applying downward force while generating roll torque to continuously tighten an M8 bolt into a rigid workpiece, along with the corresponding torque profile.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Outlook
sections.summary: FAM-DQ is an aerial manipulator that leverages its central frame as a lever to achieve high torque output and 6-DoF decoupled control in a lightweight footprint. Trajectory tracking and screw-driving experiments verified its practicality. Future work will target mechanical efficiency optimization and advanced control strategies for dynamic environments.
sections.details:
This paper presented FAM-DQ, a fully actuated aerial manipulator designed for high-torque physical interaction tasks by connecting two propulsion modules to both ends of a central frame via passive joints.

Through dynamic modeling and a lightweight cascaded 6-DoF controller, the design achieves decoupled position and attitude control. By utilizing the central frame length as a lever arm, it neatly overcomes the torque-versus-weight trade-off seen in prior fully actuated drones. Experiments across trajectory tracking, attitude tracking, static torque output, and screw driving demonstrated high control precision and physical interaction capabilities.

Looking ahead, the authors plan to optimize mechanical design to enhance torque output and energy efficiency, and develop advanced control strategies suited for more complex manipulation tasks in dynamic, uncertain environments.

takeaways: Leveraging vehicle span as a physical moment arm allows a platform to combine high torque output with full actuation without adding active tilt servos.
An asymmetric passive joint topology (1 DoF on one side, 2 DoF on the other) paired with a 1-DoF end-effector servo is a smart way to avoid kinematic singularities while minimizing parasitic mass.
Delivering over 1 N·m from a 0.447 kg platform (2.28 N·m/kg torque-to-mass ratio) provides a viable design path for industrial maintenance drones handling aerial bolting or valve turning.
limitations: Inter-module communication relies on a wireless link with ~10 ms latency, limiting control bandwidth and robustness against severe contact disturbances.
All tests were conducted in an indoor motion-capture environment; performance and stability under wind disturbances outdoors or with onboard state estimation remain unverified.
While the bolt-tightening demo succeeded, handling complex dynamic contact scenarios—such as screw cross-threading or stall recovery requiring impedance/admittance control—remains future work.
